section.title: The Altar and the Courtyard Built
section.sectionRationale: Bezalel completes the bronze altar and the courtyard that surrounds the tabernacle, including a striking note that the bronze basin was made from mirrors donated by serving women, and the chapter closes with a full, transparent inventory of all the gold, silver, and bronze used in the entire project.
section.thesis: Bezalel builds the bronze altar, the basin from women's mirrors, and the linen courtyard exactly as commanded, and Moses records a precise, public accounting of every talent and shekel of gold, silver, and bronze used in the tabernacle's construction.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the bronze altar of burnt offering; the bronze basin made from the mirrors of serving women; the courtyard enclosing the tabernacle; and the full, itemized inventory of gold, silver, and bronze.

units.label: The bronze altar
units.note: boards, so that it was hollow

media.alt: A bronze basin reflecting light near a tent entrance
media.caption: The bronze basin is cast from the mirrors of women who served at the tent entrance.

verses.text: Bezalel constructed the altar of burnt offering from acacia wood. It was square, five cubits long, five cubits wide, and three cubits high.
He made a horn at each of its four corners, so that the horns and altar were of one piece, and he overlaid the altar with bronze.
He made all the altar's utensils of bronze, its pots, shovels, sprinkling bowls, meat forks, and firepans.
He made a grate of bronze mesh for the altar under its ledge, halfway up from the bottom.
At the four corners of the bronze grate he cast four rings as holders for the poles.
And he made the poles of acacia wood and overlaid them with bronze.
Then he inserted the poles into the rings on the sides of the altar for carrying it. He made the altar with boards so that it was hollow.

units.label: The basin from the mirrors
units.note: the women who served at the entrance

verses.text: Next he made the bronze basin and its stand from the {{mirrors|mirrors}} of the women who served at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting.
Then he constructed the courtyard. The south side of the courtyard was a hundred cubits long and had curtains of finely spun linen,
with twenty posts and twenty bronze bases, and with silver hooks and bands on the posts.
The north side was also a hundred cubits long, with twenty posts and twenty bronze bases. The hooks and bands of the posts were silver.
The west side was fifty cubits long and had curtains, with ten posts and ten bases. The hooks and bands of the posts were silver.
And the east side, toward the sunrise, was also fifty cubits long.
The curtains on one side of the entrance were fifteen cubits long, with three posts and three bases.
And the curtains on the other side were also fifteen cubits long, with three posts and three bases as well.
All the curtains around the courtyard were made of finely spun linen.
The bases for the posts were bronze, the hooks and bands were silver, and the plating for the tops of the posts was silver. So all the posts of the courtyard were banded with silver.

The curtain for the entrance to the courtyard was embroidered with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and finely spun linen. It was twenty cubits long and, like the curtains of the courtyard, five cubits high,
with four posts and four bronze bases. Their hooks were silver, as well as the bands and the plating of their tops.
All the tent pegs for the tabernacle and for the surrounding courtyard were bronze.

units.label: The inventory
units.note: everything just as the LORD had commanded Moses

verses.text: This is the {{inventory|inventory}} for the tabernacle, the tabernacle of the Testimony, as recorded at Moses' command by the Levites under the direction of Ithamar son of Aaron the priest.
Bezalel son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah, made everything that the LORD had commanded Moses.
With him was Oholiab son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan, an engraver, designer, and embroiderer in blue, purple, and scarlet yarn and fine linen.
All the gold from the wave offering used for the work on the sanctuary totaled 29 talents and 730 shekels, according to the sanctuary shekel.
The silver from those numbered among the congregation totaled 100 talents and 1,775 shekels, according to the sanctuary shekel,
a beka per person, that is, half a shekel, according to the sanctuary shekel, from everyone twenty years of age or older who had crossed over to be numbered, a total of 603,550 men.
The hundred talents of silver were used to cast the bases of the sanctuary and the bases of the veil, 100 bases from the 100 talents, one talent per base.
With the 1,775 shekels of silver he made the hooks for the posts, overlaid their tops, and supplied bands for them.
The bronze from the wave offering totaled 70 talents and 2,400 shekels.
He used it to make the bases for the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, the bronze altar and its bronze grating, all the utensils for the altar,
the bases for the surrounding courtyard and its gate, and all the tent pegs for the tabernacle and its surrounding courtyard.

mirrors.gloss: Mirrors, polished bronze surfaces used for one's reflection. Women who served at the tent entrance gave up these valuable personal items to be melted down into the basin priests used for washing, turning an object of self-regard into an instrument of purification.

inventory.gloss: An accounting, inventory, or reckoning. This detailed public record of every talent and shekel used in the tabernacle's construction demonstrates transparent, accountable stewardship of what the people had generously given to God.

basic.context: Bezalel finishes the bronze altar and the basin, remarkably made from the bronze mirrors of women who served at the tent entrance, then completes the linen courtyard surrounding the whole structure. The chapter closes with a full, public accounting of exactly how much gold, silver, and bronze was used, down to the shekel.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a historical record of construction and careful financial accounting, not a text requiring symbolic decoding at every point. Its significance lies in two clear, plain truths: sacrificial giving, even of personal items like mirrors, and transparent stewardship of what God's people had entrusted for His work.
basic.originalLanguages: The basin was cast from mar'ah, mirrors, belonging to women serving at the tabernacle entrance, a striking detail of personal sacrifice turned toward purification. The chapter's detailed pequdim, inventory or accounting, shows every talent and shekel of gold, silver, and bronze publicly recorded and traced to its use.
basic.typology: The mirrors given up for the basin of washing anticipate the way believers now surrender self-regard for the sake of purification and service, looking not at their own reflection but toward Christ. The public, transparent inventory anticipates the New Testament's emphasis on trustworthy, accountable stewardship of what God's people give for His work.
basic.christ: Paul writes that believers now behold the Lord's glory as in a mirror and are transformed into the same image, 2 Corinthians 3:18, using imagery that echoes this very basin, turning attention away from self and toward Christ's glory. The careful, honest accounting of the offering foreshadows the integrity Paul insists on in handling gifts given for the Lord's work, 2 Corinthians 8:20-21.
basic.god: God cares about ordinary, personal sacrifices, women's mirrors becoming an instrument of purification, and He cares about careful, honest accounting of what has been given to Him. Nothing about serving God, however small or however financial, is exempt from both wholehearted devotion and scrupulous integrity.
basic.crossReferences: 2 Corinthians 3:18 speaks of believers beholding the Lord's glory as in a mirror and being transformed. 2 Corinthians 8:20-21 insists on transparent, honest handling of financial gifts given for ministry. 1 Corinthians 4:2 says stewards are required to be found faithful.
basic.oneStory: Women give up their mirrors, instruments of self-regard, to make a basin for purification, and Moses ensures every gift given for the tabernacle is publicly, honestly accounted for. This pattern of sacrificial devotion and transparent stewardship continues in the church, where believers turn from self toward Christ and handle what is given for His work with integrity.

context.literary:
Chapter 37 worked inside the tent; chapter 38 steps out into the open court. It moves outward in rings. First comes the great altar of burnt offering, verses 1 to 7, then the basin, verse 8, both standing in the courtyard. Then the courtyard enclosure itself, its linen curtains, posts, hooks and bands, verses 9 to 19, and finally the humblest items of all, the bronze tent pegs that held everything down, verse 20. With the pegs the building work is complete, and the narrator pauses to take stock before the garments of chapter 39.

The inventory of verses 21 to 31 opens with its own heading, 'This is the inventory for the tabernacle,' verse 21, and closes by returning to the bases and tent pegs, verse 31, where the construction account just ended. It looks back over the whole project. It names the builders again, Bezalel of Judah and Oholiab of Dan, verses 22 and 23, recalling Exodus 31:2-6 and 35:30-35, and then weighs the three metals in descending order of value: gold, silver, bronze. That order runs in reverse to the order of approach. The bronze is what every worshiper would see and touch; the gold was seen only by priests.

Two details stand out because the instructions did not contain them. The command for the basin in Exodus 30:17-21 gives neither dimensions nor the source of its metal. Chapter 38 still gives no dimensions, but it adds that the basin was made 'from the mirrors of the women who served at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting,' verse 8. A single verse, with no measurements at all, carries one of the most human notes in the whole building account. And the census figure of verse 26, 603,550 men, connects the silver of the sanctuary to the half shekel ransom commanded in Exodus 30:11-16, tying the building to the people who were counted and redeemed.
context.historical:
The altar was large: five cubits square and three high, which the BSB footnote puts at about seven and a half feet square and four and a half feet high. It was a hollow frame of acacia boards overlaid with bronze, verse 7, light enough to carry on poles. Some have suggested that at each encampment it was filled with earth or stones, in keeping with the earlier command, 'You are to make for Me an altar of earth,' Exodus 20:24; the text does not say. Its fire was to be kept burning continually, Leviticus 6:13.

Mirrors in the ancient world were discs of polished bronze or copper, not glass; Elihu speaks of the skies as 'a mirror of bronze,' Job 37:18. For women in a camp that had come out of Egypt, a mirror was a personal and valuable possession. These women are described as those 'who served at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting,' verse 8, and 1 Samuel 2:22 mentions women with the same description at Shiloh generations later, which shows that such service became an established role.

The courtyard measured a hundred cubits by fifty, about one hundred fifty by seventy five feet, with linen curtains five cubits, about seven and a half feet, high, verse 18. A man standing outside could not easily see in. There was one entrance, on the east side toward the sunrise, a twenty cubit embroidered screen, verses 13 to 18.

The inventory is remarkably exact. The gold totalled 29 talents and 730 shekels, which the BSB footnote puts at about one metric ton. The silver totalled 100 talents and 1,775 shekels. The arithmetic confirms the text: 603,550 men paying half a shekel each gives 301,775 shekels, which is 100 talents and 1,775 shekels if a talent is 3,000 shekels. The hundred talents made a hundred bases, verse 27: forty under the south frames, forty under the north, sixteen at the rear, Exodus 36:24-30, and four for the posts of the veil, Exodus 36:36. The numbers of chapter 36 and chapter 38 fit exactly. The accounting was recorded 'by the Levites under the direction of Ithamar son of Aaron,' verse 21, the priest who would later supervise the Gershonites and Merarites who carried these very curtains, frames and bases, Numbers 4:28 and 4:33.
context.canonical:
The bronze altar reappears in a sobering way after the rebellion of Korah. The bronze censers of the men who died were hammered into sheets to overlay the altar, 'a reminder to the Israelites that no outsider who is not a descendant of Aaron should approach to offer incense,' Numbers 16:38-40. The altar that received gifts also came to carry a warning. Its horns became a place of refuge, as when Adonijah fled and took 'hold of the horns of the altar,' 1 Kings 1:50.

The basin is enlarged in Solomon's temple into the great cast bronze Sea, 1 Kings 7:23, with ten further basins. The women who served at the entrance appear again at Shiloh, 1 Samuel 2:22, where their abuse by Eli's sons marks the corruption of the priesthood. In the New Testament, Anna 'never left the temple, but worshiped night and day, fasting and praying,' Luke 2:37, and she is among the first to recognize the infant Christ.

The accounting of verses 21 to 31 sets a standard followed in later building and repair. Under Joash the men handling the temple money needed no audit 'because they acted with integrity,' 2 Kings 12:15, and the same is said under Josiah, 2 Kings 22:7. When Ezra carried gold and silver back to Jerusalem, 'everything was verified by number and weight, and the total weight was recorded,' Ezra 8:34. Paul brings the same care to the collection for Jerusalem, 'not only in the eyes of the Lord, but also in the eyes of men,' 2 Corinthians 8:21.

The half shekel of verse 26 continues as the annual temple tax of Jesus' day, the two drachmas collectors asked Peter about, Matthew 17:24-27. And the altar itself finds its fulfillment when Hebrews says, 'We have an altar from which those who serve at the tabernacle have no right to eat,' Hebrews 13:10, because Jesus 'suffered outside the city gate, to sanctify the people by His own blood,' Hebrews 13:12.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wants the first hearers to see three things. First, the way into God's presence begins with sacrifice and washing. The first objects a worshiper met after passing through the single gate were the altar and the basin, and the chapter places them first. No one reached the tent without passing blood and water. Second, the sanctuary belonged to all the people. Every counted man's half shekel stood under its frames; the women's mirrors formed its basin; ordinary bronze held down its tent pegs. The inventory ensures that no gift is lost from view. Third, the people's gifts were handled honestly. By recording the totals under priestly supervision and publishing them, Moses lets Israel verify that what they gave was used for what they gave it for.

For a people who had recently seen gold vanish into a calf, Exodus 32:24, the careful weighing of every talent would have been reassuring. The author presents leadership that can be trusted with holy things, and a God whose house is built from the whole people's gifts and accounted for before the whole people.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes Israel's altar, basin, courtyard and accounts. It does not require churches to build altars, use bronze or publish their books in this format. The altar and basin belonged to a system of sacrifice and ritual washing which the New Testament declares fulfilled in Christ's 'one sacrifice for sins,' Hebrews 10:12.

What carries forward is taught elsewhere in Scripture and illustrated here. Those who handle gifts given for God's work must be found faithful, 1 Corinthians 4:2, and should take care to do right in the sight of others, 2 Corinthians 8:20-21. Gifts of every size matter to God, as Jesus showed when He commended the widow's two small coins, Mark 12:41-44. And the equal half shekel from rich and poor, Exodus 30:15, reflects a truth the gospel states outright: before God 'there is no distinction,' Romans 3:22.

debates.question: Why does the text specifically note that the basin was made from women's mirrors, rather than simply saying it was made of bronze?

views.label: Highlighting sacrificial devotion
views.case: Many interpreters see the detail as honouring the women's devotion. A mirror was a personal, valued possession, and giving it up for the basin where priests washed before approaching God turned an object of self-regard into an instrument of consecration. The detail is not in the instructions of Exodus 30:17-21, so the narrator added it on purpose.

views.label: A historical note about the source of the bronze
views.case: Others read it as an accurate record of where suitable bronze came from, without a moral lesson intended. Polished bronze mirrors were an obvious source of high quality metal, and the text itself does not contrast vanity with purity.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree that real women gave real possessions of value, and that Scripture thought it worth recording. Whether or not a contrast between self-regard and cleansing is intended, the detail honours their gift and their service at the tent.

debates.question: Who were 'the women who served at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting,' when the tabernacle had not yet been built?

views.label: Women serving at the earlier tent
views.case: Before the tabernacle existed Moses used to pitch a tent outside the camp and call it 'the Tent of Meeting,' Exodus 33:7. Women who gathered there to seek the LORD could be described this way at the time the basin was made.

views.label: A description from the narrator's later vantage
views.case: The narrator may be identifying the women by the role they came to hold, the same role mentioned at Shiloh in 1 Samuel 2:22. The verb for 'served' is the one used for Levitical service at the tent in Numbers 4:23, which suggests an organized ministry that continued after the tabernacle stood.

views.label: Women who served during the building
views.case: Some suggest the phrase describes women who assisted with the work at the site of the tent while it was being made, much as skilled women spun the yarn and goat hair, Exodus 35:25-26.

debates.bearing: The text does not define their duties, and any answer goes beyond it. What is clear is that women had a recognized place of service at the entrance to God's house from the beginning, and that their gift was built into the basin every priest used.

study.originalLanguages:
The altar is mizbach, from the verb zabach, to slaughter for sacrifice, so the very name means place of sacrifice. Its full title in verse 1 is 'the altar of burnt offering,' and the burnt offering is the olah, from the verb alah, to go up. The offering was the one that went up whole in smoke to God.

At each corner stood a 'horn,' qeren, verse 2, 'of one piece' with the altar. The horn is Scripture's common image of strength, as in 'the horn of my salvation,' Psalm 18:2, and Zechariah's song that God 'has raised up a horn of salvation for us,' Luke 1:69. Blood was applied to the horns in sacrifice, and a fugitive could grasp them for mercy, 1 Kings 1:50.

The women of verse 8 'served,' a participle of tsaba. The root is the one behind tsaba, 'host' or 'army,' and so behind the title 'LORD of Hosts.' Its basic sense is organized service, and it is the verb used of the Levites who 'serve in the work at the Tent of Meeting,' Numbers 4:23. The same participle describes the women at Shiloh in 1 Samuel 2:22. The women are not casual bystanders; their service is named with the vocabulary of ordered ministry. The Septuagint renders the phrase as women who fasted at the doors of the tent, the kind of devotion Luke later describes in Anna, 'fasting and praying,' Luke 2:37.

The 'mirrors' are marot, the plural of marah, from raah, to see. The very same plural means 'visions' in Ezekiel 1:1, 'I saw visions of God.' What the women gave up was literally their 'seeings,' the objects in which they saw themselves; they were melted into the basin that prepared priests to serve before the One whom no one may see and live, Exodus 33:20.

The gold and bronze are called tenuphah, 'wave offering,' verses 24 and 29, a gift presented by lifting or moving it before the LORD, the same term used of the gold in Exodus 35:22. The silver is described differently, as coming 'from those numbered among the congregation,' verse 25. The gold and bronze were gifts; the silver was ransom, the kopher of Exodus 30:12, 'a ransom for his life.'

The 'beka' of verse 26 comes from baqa, to split, and means a half, 'half a shekel' as the verse explains. It is the weight of the gold nose ring Abraham's servant gave Rebekah, Genesis 24:22. The weights are 'according to the sanctuary shekel,' verses 24 to 26, a standard fixed at twenty gerahs, Exodus 30:13, so that every Israelite's half shekel weighed the same.

Finally, verse 21 calls the whole structure 'the tabernacle of the Testimony,' mishkan haedut. The edut is the covenant testimony placed in the ark, Exodus 25:16. The whole building, from the silver bases to the pegs, is named for the covenant it housed. Stephen uses the same title, 'the tabernacle of the Testimony,' Acts 7:44, and Revelation sees 'the tabernacle of the Testimony' opened in heaven, Revelation 15:5.

typology.type: The bronze altar of burnt offering, Exodus 38:1-7
typology.fulfillment: The altar stood just inside the gate, and every approach to God began there with the death of a substitute, whose smoke went up whole. Hebrews says, 'We have an altar,' Hebrews 13:10, and explains that Jesus 'suffered outside the city gate, to sanctify the people by His own blood,' Hebrews 13:12. The correspondence is the way in through sacrifice; the escalation is that Israel's priests offered 'again and again the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins,' but Christ 'offered for all time one sacrifice for sins' and sat down, Hebrews 10:11-12. The type falls short because its fire had to burn continually, Leviticus 6:13; His offering is finished.

typology.type: The bronze basin for washing, Exodus 38:8
typology.fulfillment: Priests had to wash their hands and feet at the basin before entering the tent or serving at the altar, 'so that they will not die,' Exodus 30:20. The New Testament speaks of cleansing that this washing foreshadowed: God saved us 'through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit,' Titus 3:5, and believers draw near with 'our bodies washed with pure water,' Hebrews 10:22. Jesus Himself washed His disciples' feet and said, 'Unless I wash you, you have no part with Me,' John 13:8. The type falls short because the priest washed himself, repeatedly; in the gospel, Christ washes His people.

typology.type: The silver of ransom under the sanctuary, Exodus 38:25-27
typology.fulfillment: Every counted man paid the same half shekel, 'a ransom for his life,' Exodus 30:12, rich and poor alike, Exodus 30:15, and the whole sanctuary stood on that silver. Jesus came 'to give His life as a ransom for many,' Mark 10:45, and in Him the redemption is equally needed and equally free: 'There is no distinction, for all have sinned,' and all are 'justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus,' Romans 3:22-24. The type falls short because the half shekel was paid by the redeemed themselves, and again at every census; the ransom Christ paid was His own life, given once.

typology.type: The single gate of the courtyard, Exodus 38:13-18
typology.fulfillment: The courtyard had one entrance only, on the east, a twenty cubit screen of blue, purple and scarlet, verse 18. Whoever came to God came that way. Jesus says, 'I am the gate. If anyone enters through Me, he will be saved,' John 10:9, and 'No one comes to the Father except through Me,' John 14:6. The correspondence is that there is one way in; the escalation is that the gate leads not only into a courtyard but to the Father. The type falls short because the court curtains kept most people at a distance, while in the new Jerusalem the gates 'will never be shut,' Revelation 21:25.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first through the altar. It stood between the gate and the tent, so that no one reached God's dwelling without passing the place of sacrifice. Hebrews draws on exactly this when it says that Christians 'have an altar,' Hebrews 13:10. The sacrifices of the Day of Atonement were burned outside the camp, and 'so Jesus also suffered outside the city gate, to sanctify the people by His own blood,' Hebrews 13:12. The bronze altar at the door of the tabernacle becomes the cross outside the walls of Jerusalem, and the burnt offering that went up whole becomes Christ who 'gave Himself up for us as a fragrant sacrificial offering to God,' Ephesians 5:2.

It leads to Christ through the basin. The priests washed there before every act of service, and the command carried a warning, 'so that they will not die,' Exodus 30:21. Jesus, the night before His death, took a basin and washed His disciples' feet. When Peter protested, Jesus said, 'Unless I wash you, you have no part with Me,' and added, 'Whoever has already bathed needs only to wash his feet,' John 13:8-10. Paul says Christ gave Himself for the church 'to sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing with water through the word,' Ephesians 5:26. The one who is both the altar's offering and the basin's water is the same Lord.

It leads to Christ through the ransom silver. The whole sanctuary rested on a hundred silver bases, each cast from the half shekels of redeemed men, verse 27. Jesus said He came 'to give His life as a ransom for many,' Mark 10:45. There is a remarkable moment in Matthew 17:24-27 when collectors of the temple tax, the successor of this half shekel, ask whether Jesus pays. He answers that 'the sons are exempt,' for He is the Son of the house, yet He provides the coin 'for My tax and yours,' paying for Himself and for Peter together. The One who owed no ransom pays the ransom for His people.

It leads to Christ through the one gate. The courtyard had a single entrance, verse 18. Jesus is 'the gate,' John 10:9, and 'the way,' John 14:6. The embroidered screen of the gate, of the same colours as the veil, verse 18, invited all Israel to draw near through one appointed door.

It leads to Christ in the mirrors. Paul writes that believers 'with unveiled faces all reflect the glory of the Lord' and 'are being transformed into His image,' 2 Corinthians 3:18. The women gave up the bronze in which they saw themselves; in Christ believers become mirrors of His glory.

Care is needed here. The New Testament connects the altar, the washing and the ransom to Christ. It does not assign meanings to the bronze, the silver hooks or the number of posts, and readers should not make the metals into a code of their own. The links worth preaching are the ones Scripture draws.
study.god:
The chapter shows the holiness of God and His way of approach. The single gate, the high linen wall, the altar and the basin all say that God cannot be approached casually. Sin must be dealt with by sacrifice and uncleanness by washing before anyone may serve in His presence. Yet the same arrangements say that God can be approached. There is a gate, and it faces the sunrise, verse 13. The altar is at the door, not hidden. God's holiness sets the terms of access, and His grace provides the means.

It shows the impartiality of God. Every man paid the same half shekel, 'the rich shall not give more than a half shekel, nor shall the poor give less,' Exodus 30:15. The LORD is 'the great, mighty, and awesome God, showing no partiality,' Deuteronomy 10:17, and Peter learned that 'God does not show favoritism,' Acts 10:34. The foundation of God's house was laid with exactly equal gifts, because every life needed the same ransom.

It shows a God who counts and knows. The inventory numbers every talent and shekel, and the census numbers every man, 603,550 of them, verse 26. God is not vague about His people. He 'determines the number of the stars' and 'calls them each by name,' Psalm 147:4, and Jesus says that 'even the very hairs of your head are all numbered,' Matthew 10:30. The precision of the inventory reflects a God who knows each person He has redeemed.

It shows a God who honours small and personal gifts. Among the tons of gold, silver and bronze, the narrator stops to record where the basin came from: the mirrors of women who served. God noticed what they gave, and Scripture keeps their gift in view forever. Jesus did the same when He watched the treasury and singled out a widow's two coins, Mark 12:41-44.

It shows a God of truth who wants His people's gifts handled truthfully. The accounting was done at Moses' command, under a priest, by Levites, verse 21, and made public. God is not served by careless or hidden handling of what belongs to Him. Later Scripture praises those who 'acted with integrity,' 2 Kings 12:15, because honesty with holy things reflects the character of the Holy One.

For worship, the chapter teaches both reverence and gratitude. Reverence, because the way to God runs through an altar and a basin, and no one enters on their own terms. Gratitude, because the way is open, the ransom is provided, and the God who receives the mirrors of serving women receives the humble gifts of His people still.

crossReferences.note: The instructions for the bronze altar and the courtyard, which Exodus 38:1-20 carries out closely. The command ends 'just as you were shown on the mountain,' Exodus 27:8, and chapter 38 records that the altar and court were built to that pattern, measure for measure.

The half shekel ransom paid by every counted man, rich and poor alike, 'to atone for your lives,' and given 'for the service of the Tent of Meeting.' Exodus 38:25-28 shows where that silver went: into the bases, hooks and bands of the sanctuary.

The command for the basin, set between the Tent of Meeting and the altar, where Aaron and his sons washed hands and feet 'so that they will not die.' Exodus 38:8 records its making and adds a detail the command lacks, that it came from the women's mirrors.

At Shiloh, generations later, the same phrase appears: 'the women who served at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting.' Eli's sons abused them, a sign of the priesthood's corruption. The verse confirms that the role mentioned in Exodus 38:8 continued in Israel's worship.

After Korah's rebellion the bronze censers of the men who died were hammered into sheets to overlay the altar as a sign. The bronze altar of Exodus 38 thus came to carry a warning that only those God appoints may draw near with incense.

The census of fighting men totals 603,550, exactly the figure in Exodus 38:26. The silver of the sanctuary corresponds precisely to the number of Israel's counted men, each represented by his half shekel beneath the frames.

When Joash repaired the temple, the men who paid the workmen needed no audit 'because they acted with integrity.' The accountability of Exodus 38:21-31 set the pattern; later generations were measured by whether their handling of holy funds could be trusted.

Ezra's returning exiles weighed out the silver and gold for the temple, and 'everything was verified by number and weight, and the total weight was recorded.' The same exactness as Exodus 38 marks the rebuilding after exile.

Jesus is asked about the two drachma temple tax, the later form of the half shekel of Exodus 30 and 38. He says the sons are exempt, yet provides the coin for Himself and Peter, the Son of the house paying the sanctuary ransom for His disciple.

'We have an altar,' Hebrews says, and ties it to Jesus suffering outside the city gate to sanctify the people by His own blood. The bronze altar of Exodus 38 finds its fulfillment at the cross, where the one sacrifice was offered.

Believers draw near to God 'having our hearts sprinkled to cleanse us from a guilty conscience and our bodies washed with pure water.' The language of altar blood and basin water from Exodus 38 is applied to every Christian's access to God.

Anna the prophetess 'never left the temple, but worshiped night and day, fasting and praying.' She stands in the line of the women who served at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting, and she is among the first to recognize the child Jesus.

study.oneStory:
From the first pages of Scripture, sacrifice has marked the way back to God. Abel brought an offering from his flock, Genesis 4:4. Noah stepped off the ark and 'built an altar to the LORD,' Genesis 8:20. Abraham built altars across the land, and on Mount Moriah he told Isaac, 'God Himself will provide the lamb for the burnt offering, my son,' Genesis 22:8. Those altars were scattered and occasional. In Exodus 38 one altar is set at the door of God's own house, and a whole nation is taught that the way to Him runs through sacrifice.

Water too has carried meaning from the beginning. The Spirit hovered over the waters at creation; the flood washed a corrupted world; Israel passed through the sea. Now a bronze basin stands between the altar and the tent, and no priest may serve without washing. Through the prophets God promised more: 'I will also sprinkle clean water on you, and you will be clean,' Ezekiel 36:25.

The chapter also sets up the story of redemption through its silver. Every counted Israelite paid a ransom for his life, and the sanctuary stood on that ransom. The rest of the Old Testament keeps the half shekel, but it cannot settle the account for good; it must be paid at every census and later every year.

All of this reaches its goal in Christ. He is the sacrifice offered once for all, Hebrews 10:12, the ransom for many, Mark 10:45, and the one who washes His people, John 13:8. The single gate of the courtyard becomes the one who says, 'I am the gate,' John 10:9.

The story ends in a city where the pattern is completed and transformed. There is no altar in John's vision of the new Jerusalem, because the Lamb who was slain is on the throne. Nothing unclean will enter, Revelation 21:27, yet the gates stand open and 'will never be shut,' Revelation 21:25. The washing of the basin becomes the blessing of the redeemed: 'Blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they may have the right to the tree of life and may enter the city by its gates,' Revelation 22:14. The mirrors given up at Sinai point to the day when God's people will no longer see dimly but 'face to face,' 1 Corinthians 13:12.

questions: Women gave up their personal mirrors, valuable and intimate items, to become part of a basin used for purification before God. What personal possession or attachment might God be asking you to surrender for the sake of His work?
The tabernacle's finances were meticulously, publicly accounted for down to the shekel. How transparent and accountable is your own handling of money or resources given for God's purposes?

The bronze basin, once used for looking at oneself, became an instrument for washing before serving God. Where in your life could something once focused on self be repurposed toward serving and honoring God instead?

The silver came from an equal ransom paid by every man in Israel, rich or poor alike. How does remembering that your own place among God's people rests on an equal, not merit-based, provision shape your sense of belonging?

This chapter closes an enormous building project with careful bookkeeping rather than a dramatic celebration. Where in your own life do you need to value the quiet, careful, administrative faithfulness that keeps God's work honest and trustworthy?

translationNotes.note: The mirrors of the women who served at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting is a brief but notable detail; these were likely polished bronze surfaces used as mirrors, and the identity and specific service of these women is not further elaborated here, though similar language appears in 1 Samuel 2:22.

The tabernacle of the Testimony emphasizes the ark and its covenant tablets as the defining feature of the whole structure, even as this verse turns to a detailed financial inventory rather than further furnishing description.
The total of 603,550 men corresponds exactly to the census figure recorded in Numbers 1:46, confirming this financial accounting reflects the same historical census commanded in Exodus 30:11-16.
